question: How many old ReplicaSets does a Deployment keep around by default so that it can be rolled back?
expected_answer: 10, controlled by .spec.revisionHistoryLimit.
evidence_quote: You can set `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` field in a Deployment to specify how many old ReplicaSets for this Deployment you want to retain. The rest will be garbage-collected in the background. By default, it is 10.

question: During a Deployment rolling update, is it allowed to set both maxSurge and maxUnavailable to zero?
expected_answer: No. maxUnavailable cannot be 0 when maxSurge is 0.
gold_heading: Writing a Deployment Spec > Strategy > Rolling Update Deployment > Max Unavailable
evidence_quote: `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` is an optional field that specifies the maximum number of Pods that can be unavailable during the update process. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5) or a percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The absolute number is calculated from percentage by rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is 0.

question: When the number of replicas is reduced, how can I influence which Pods get removed first?
expected_answer: Set the controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost annotation on the Pod; the Pod with the lower value is removed first.
gold_heading: Working with ReplicaSets > Pod deletion cost
evidence_quote: Using the `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost` annotation, users can set a preference regarding which pods to remove first when downscaling a ReplicaSet.

question: For a StatefulSet, which PersistentVolumeClaim retention setting deletes claims only for the replicas that were scaled down?
expected_answer: whenScaled: Delete. (whenDeleted applies when the whole StatefulSet is deleted.)
evidence_quote: With the `whenDeleted` policy all PVCs from the `volumeClaimTemplate` are deleted after their Pods have been deleted. With the `whenScaled` policy, only PVCs corresponding to Pod replicas being scaled down are deleted, after their Pods have been deleted.

question: How many times does a Job retry failed Pods by default before the Job is marked as failed?
expected_answer: 6 (.spec.backoffLimit), unless backoffLimitPerIndex is specified.
gold_heading: Handling Pod and container failures > Pod backoff failure policy
evidence_quote: The `.spec.backoffLimit` is set by default to 6, unless the backoff limit per index (only Indexed Job) is specified. When `.spec.backoffLimitPerIndex` is specified, then `.spec.backoffLimit` defaults to 2147483647 (MaxInt32).

question: A CronJob is set not to allow concurrent runs. What happens when the next scheduled time arrives while the previous Job is still running?
expected_answer: The CronJob skips the new Job run (concurrencyPolicy: Forbid).
gold_heading: Writing a CronJob spec > Concurrency policy
evidence_quote: `Forbid`: The CronJob does not allow concurrent runs; if it is time for a new Job run and the previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob skips the new Job run.

question: How can I make finished batch Jobs, whether they succeeded or failed, clean themselves up after a while?
expected_answer: Set .spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished on the Job (handled by the TTL-after-finished controller).
evidence_quote: You can use this mechanism to clean up finished Jobs (either `Complete` or `Failed`) automatically by specifying the `.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` field of a Job, as in this example.

question: While a slow-starting container is still covered by a startup probe, which other health checks does Kubernetes hold back?
expected_answer: Liveness and readiness probes are not run until the startup probe succeeds.
evidence_quote: If a startup probe is configured, Kubernetes does not execute liveness or readiness probes until the startup probe succeeds, allowing the application time to finish its initialization.

question: What happens to the Pod as a whole if one of its init containers fails during startup and the Pod's restartPolicy is Never?
expected_answer: Kubernetes treats the overall Pod as failed.
evidence_quote: If a Pod's init container fails, the kubelet repeatedly restarts that init container until it succeeds. However, if the Pod has a `restartPolicy` of Never, and an init container fails during startup of that Pod, Kubernetes treats the overall Pod as failed.

question: How do I declare a helper container that starts before the application containers but keeps running for the whole life of the Pod?
expected_answer: Define it under initContainers with restartPolicy: Always (a sidecar container).
evidence_quote: If an init container is created with its `restartPolicy` set to `Always`, it will start and remain running during the entire life of the Pod. This can be helpful for running supporting services separated from the main application containers.

question: What must hold for every container's CPU and memory requests and limits for a Pod to be given the Guaranteed QoS class?
expected_answer: Every container has CPU and memory limits and requests, all greater than zero, with each limit equal to its request.
gold_heading: Quality of Service classes > Guaranteed > Criteria
evidence_quote: Every Container in the Pod must have a memory limit and a memory request, both greater than zero. * For every Container in the Pod, the memory limit must equal the memory request. * Every Container in the Pod must have a CPU limit and a CPU request, both greater than zero. * For every Container in the Pod, the CPU limit must equal the CPU request.

question: By default, how far can the ratio of current to desired metric value drift from 1.0 before the HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes the number of replicas?
expected_answer: Within a tolerance of 0.1 it does nothing (the tolerance is configurable).
gold_heading: How does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler work? > Algorithm details
evidence_quote: The control plane skips any scaling action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a configurable tolerance, 0.1 by default).

question: What DNS name pattern does an ordinary (non-headless) Service get, and what does that name resolve to?
expected_answer: my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example, resolving to the Service's cluster IP.
evidence_quote: (not headless) Services are assigned DNS A and/or AAAA records, depending on the IP family or families of the Service, with a name of the form `my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example`. This resolves to the cluster IP of the Service.

question: What happens if a path in an Ingress rule does not specify a path type?
expected_answer: The Ingress fails validation: every path must have a pathType.
evidence_quote: Each path in an Ingress is required to have a corresponding path type. Paths that do not include an explicit `pathType` will fail validation.

question: If no network policy applies to a pod, may that pod open outbound connections to any destination?
expected_answer: Yes. By default a pod is non-isolated for egress and all outbound connections are allowed.
gold_heading: The two sorts of pod isolation
evidence_quote: By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed. A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has "Egress" in its `policyTypes`

question: How many endpoints can one EndpointSlice hold by default, and what controls that limit?
expected_answer: 100 by default; set with the kube-controller-manager flag --max-endpoints-per-slice (maximum 1000).
evidence_quote: By default, the control plane creates and manages EndpointSlices to have no more than 100 endpoints each. You can configure this with the `--max-endpoints-per-slice` kube-controller-manager flag, up to a maximum of 1000.

question: How does Kubernetes lower the risk that a manually chosen Service IP clashes with one assigned automatically?
expected_answer: The ClusterIP range is split into bands: dynamic allocation uses the upper band first, leaving the lower band for static assignments.
gold_heading: How can you avoid Service ClusterIP conflicts?
evidence_quote: Dynamic IP assignment uses the upper band by default, once this has been exhausted it will use the lower range. This will allow users to use static allocations on the lower band with a low risk of collision.

question: How do I create a Service that has no virtual IP, so that clients get the individual Pod addresses from DNS instead?
expected_answer: Create a headless Service: type ClusterIP with .spec.clusterIP set to None.
evidence_quote: To define a headless Service, you make a Service with `.spec.type` set to ClusterIP (which is also the default for `type`), and you additionally set `.spec.clusterIP` to None.

question: How many policy types may I choose for a group of Pods, and which ones exist?
expected_answer: Exactly one of two: `basic` or `gang`.
evidence_quote: The `schedulingPolicy` field supports two policy types: `basic` and `gang`. You must specify exactly one.

question: Can I write an integer priority directly into a Pod's spec, or must it come from somewhere else?
expected_answer: No. Assign a PriorityClass; Kubernetes sets .spec.priority from it.
evidence_quote: If you assign a priority class to a Pod, Kubernetes sets the `.spec.priority` field for that Pod based on the PriorityClass you specified (you cannot set `.spec.priority` directly).

question: How is the hostname of each replica in an ordered, stateful set of Pods constructed?
expected_answer: <statefulset name>-<ordinal>, for example web-0, web-1, web-2.
evidence_quote: Each Pod in a StatefulSet derives its hostname from the name of the StatefulSet and the ordinal of the Pod. The pattern for the constructed hostname is `$(statefulset name)-$(ordinal)`.

question: Which networking modes are available for containers on Windows nodes?
expected_answer: L2bridge, L2tunnel, Overlay (Beta), Transparent and NAT.
evidence_quote: Windows supports five different networking drivers/modes: L2bridge, L2tunnel, Overlay (Beta), Transparent, and NAT.

question: How can I tell that a Pod in the kube-system namespace is a mirror of a node-managed control plane Pod?
expected_answer: It carries the kubernetes.io/config.mirror annotation.
evidence_quote: If your cluster runs control plane components as Pods, they are likely static Pods. You can recognize their mirror Pods in the `kube-system` namespace by the `kubernetes.io/config.mirror` annotation.

question: Why can't I use kubectl edit to attach a temporary debugging container to a running Pod?
expected_answer: Ephemeral containers are added through the special ephemeralcontainers API handler, not by editing pod.spec.
gold_heading: Understanding ephemeral containers > What is an ephemeral container?
evidence_quote: Ephemeral containers are created using a special `ephemeralcontainers` handler in the API rather than by adding them directly to `pod.spec`, so it's not possible to add an ephemeral container using `kubectl edit`.

question: If a Pod is configured to run in its own user namespace, can it also share the node's network namespace?
expected_answer: No. With hostUsers: false you may not set hostNetwork, hostIPC or hostPID to true.
evidence_quote: if you set `hostUsers: false` then you are not allowed to set any of: * `hostNetwork: true` * `hostIPC: true` * `hostPID: true`

question: Is a kernel panic on a node a voluntary or an involuntary disruption for the Pods running there?
expected_answer: Involuntary: it is an unavoidable hardware or system software error.
evidence_quote: We call these unavoidable cases *involuntary disruptions* to an application. Examples are: - a hardware failure of the physical machine backing the node - cluster administrator deletes VM (instance) by mistake - cloud provider or hypervisor failure makes VM disappear - a kernel panic

question: Can I set a Pod's hostnameOverride to a 100-character name?
expected_answer: No. The value is limited to 64 characters and must follow the RFC 1123 DNS subdomain standard.
evidence_quote: The `hostnameOverride` field has a length limitation of 64 characters and must adhere to the DNS subdomain names standard defined in RFC 1123.

question: If one of my nodes has no zone label, will a Service's traffic still be kept inside the zone it came from?
expected_answer: No. The control plane sets no topology hints, so kube-proxy does not filter endpoints by zone.
evidence_quote: If any node does not have a `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` label or is not reporting a value for allocatable CPU, the control plane does not set any topology-aware endpoint hints and so kube-proxy does not filter endpoints by zone.

question: Which disruption mode is applied to a group of Pods when I don't choose one?
expected_answer: Single.
evidence_quote: The API supports two disruption modes: `Single` and `All`. The default one is `Single`.

question: Which ingress controllers are supported and maintained by the Kubernetes project itself?
expected_answer: The AWS and GCE ingress controllers.
evidence_quote: Kubernetes as a project supports and maintains AWS, and GCE ingress controllers.
